source.title: TOFU: A Task of Fictitious Unlearning for LLMs
source.authors: Pratyush Maini; Zhi-Li Feng; Avi Schwarzschild; Zachary Chase Lipton; J. Kolter

record.tranche_reason: The study tests several unlearning baselines on a controlled question-answering task and reports that they generally fail to achieve strong forgetting while preserving utility.
record.gate_note: The paper reports results for its unlearning baselines, including forget-quality tests and utility measurements. It does not test fine-tuning as a recovery attack, activation-direction ablation, quantization, or prompt-based recovery. The cited Harry Potter and prompting findings are from other work and are not rows. The initial finetuning results show the benchmark teaches target facts, but are not results about post-unlearning recovery.
record.test_reason: The study runs four unlearning methods on Llama-2-7B and Phi-1.5. It measures whether the forget set becomes indistinguishable from a never-trained retain model (KS-test on Truth Ratio) while utility is kept. That bears directly on the forgetting-plus-utility part of version A. It runs no recovery attacks, so versions B–F are untested.
record.authors_conclusion: Broadly correct. The authors conclude the four baseline methods are largely unsuccessful: strong forget quality is hard to reach without substantial utility loss, and flaws show only across several metrics. In the discussion they also argue, without testing it, that such methods change outputs for specific prompts rather than removing the information.
record.recipe_differences: The paper tests four baseline unlearning objectives on synthetic fictitious-author data, including Gradient Ascent, but does not reproduce an original-source method-and-attack setup. It uses Truth Ratio distributions and a KS-test for forget quality, plus utility metrics; it tests no post-unlearning recovery attack.
record.method_sensitivity: Results depend on forget-set size: the paper reports different forgetting/utility trade-offs for 1% versus larger 5% and 10% sets. It also reports that continued unlearning up to 10 epochs does not help the baseline methods on the 1% set.
record.problems: The tested data are synthetic fictitious-author facts learned during finetuning, not knowledge acquired during pretraining. The paper's forget-quality conclusion relies on Truth Ratio and a KS-test as an approximation to indistinguishability, and it notes that gibberish outputs can yield misleadingly strong forget quality. Many trajectory values are shown in figures rather than tabulated. The study does not test the recovery attacks named in the claim.
record.rows_left_out: The study's detailed per-method and per-severity trajectory values in Figures 5–6 and Figures 10–33 are not separately transcribed; the text provides aggregate statements for the reported outcomes. The continued-unlearning result in Appendix D concerns whether more unlearning epochs improve the same baseline methods, not one of the claim's recovery attacks.

untested.parts: Whether simple attacks recover the forgotten knowledge after unlearning; accuracy relative to chance is not measured (indistinguishability from a retain model is used instead).
All: no relearning or fine-tuning attack after unlearning.
All: no activation ablation or internal analysis.
All: no prompting, jailbreak or in-context recovery. Paraphrased answers are used only inside the Truth Ratio metric.
All: no robust method is proposed or tested.

missing.what: Continued unlearning to 10 epochs on the Phi-1.5 1% set: no method crosses the 0.05 p-value threshold.
Fine-grained utility for Gradient Difference on Llama-2-7B, 5% set: Retain-set and Real-Authors ROUGE fall with the forget set, while World Facts stay relatively unchanged (knowledge entanglement).
Some Gradient Ascent checkpoints come very close to the retain model in forget quality, but the authors caveat that gibberish models can score this way.

record.verdict_notes: This is a benchmark paper on synthetic fictitious-author facts learned during fine-tuning, not pretraining knowledge. Its forget-quality metric (KS-test against a retain model) is stricter than the 'near chance' accuracy named in version A, so incomplete forgetting here does not imply that knowledge is extractable by an attack. No recovery attack is run. The paper is not an original source.

versions.untested_parts: The study does not test simple attacks after unlearning, and does not measure whether targeted-knowledge accuracy reaches chance specifically. It evaluates forget quality using Truth Ratio distributions and a KS-test, alongside model utility.

rows.measure: Forget quality: KS-test p-value comparing Truth Ratio distributions with the retain model
rows.value: all of these p-values are less than 0.001
rows.note: The paper reports this result collectively for the methods, not as separate numerical values. The low p-values indicate the unlearned models remain distinguishable from the retain model.
rows.check: On the 1% set, trajectories move up in forget quality with stable utility, but every p-value stays below 0.001. The authors say 'approach strong forgetting' yet none cross 0.05. That is incomplete forgetting, not none, so the state should be partial rather than absent.

relation.reason: Its own results bear on forgetting plus utility, part of version A.

tranche.reason: Its own results show the baseline methods (including GA) fail to give indistinguishable forgetting with utility kept. That makes version A partial or wrong in this setting. T3 is also defensible.

source_check.notes: Unlearning starts from Llama-2-7B and Phi-1.5 base models finetuned on all TOFU data (the paper's 'base models'). Forget quality is a KS-test p-value against a retain model: higher is better, threshold 0.05. Results are pooled over four methods with no per-method numbers. The 10-epoch test is Phi 1% only (Fig 9). No recovery attacks. r5/r6 largely duplicate r3/r4.

statements.correction: Optional precision: TOFU, four baseline methods (GA, GD, KL, PO), 5 epochs. 1% forget set: utility stable, forget-quality p-value <0.001 (Phi-1.5) and ≤0.01 (Llama-2-7B), all below the 0.05 threshold. 5%/10% sets: severe utility drops, and high-forget-quality models are unusable.
statements.problem: None for this study. '≤0.01' is a loose but true bound for both models (Phi <0.001, Llama never above 0.01). 'Collapse' matches 'severe drops' and 'unusable'. The SimNPO, LLaMA-3.1 and retraining parts are about other studies. The sentence does not say that TOFU results are pooled over four baseline methods.
